la:noun:annus.html:
annus, i, m.
acc. to some, as Corssen, Beitr. 16, for am-nus, from 2. an- am-; or acc. to others, directly from 2. anus, a ring, and kindred to the form appearing, in ἐνοαυτός, δί-ενος, τρί-ενος
.
Lit., a circuit, circular course, periodical return: tempus a brumā ad brumam, dum sol redit, vocatur annus; quod, ut parvi circuli anuli, sic magni dicebantur circites ani, unde annus, Müll.; cf. for the same idea: circum tribus actis annis,: anno, qui solstitiali circumagitur orbe,; : quae (stellae) volvunt magnos in magnis orbibus annos,; so : multis solis redeuntibus annis,; so ; cf. also Voss ad ; and the Heb. = month, from = to renew; hence, a year (consisting among the Rom. orig. of ten months, ending with Dec. and beginning with Mart., but from the time of Numa of twelve): annos sexaginta natus,: principio circum tribus actis impiger annis Floret equus,: tempora mutare annorum,the seasons,: anni tempus, Varr, R. R. 1, 46: nemo est tam senex, qui se annum non putet posse vivere,: centum et septem complevit annos, et saep.: anni fugaces,: anni mobiles,: annus piger,: anni breves,: per exactos annos,: initio anni,: principio anni,: anno ineunte,; : anno exeunte,: extremo anno,: extremo anni,: anno circumacto,: vertente anno,: annus totus,: annus solidus,a full year,.—Poet.: pleno anno,at the close of,; ; : nondum centum et decem anni sunt, cum lata est lex,: lex anno post quam lata sit abrogata, id. Cornel. Fragm. ap. Orell. IV. 2, p. 448.—
Adverb. phrases.
Anno.
A year ago, last year, πέρυσι (for the most part anteclass.; not used by Cic.),: quattuor minis ego emi istanc anno,; : utrum anno an horno te abstuleris a viro, Lucil. ap. ; so, ab anno priore,; and: ab anno praeterito,.—
A full or whole year, : corpus ejus matronae anno luxerunt, (in Livy, instead of it, annum; v. 2. infra).—
In each year, yearly: uno boum jugo conseri anno quadragena jugera, difficilis tricena justum est,.—But in is freq. added when it is related how often a thing happened during the year, : ter in anno,: semel in anno, (cf.: semel per annum,) al. (but without in' ter et quater anno, : bis anno,).—
Annum, a year, during a whole year: matronae annum eum luxerunt,.—
Ad annum, for the coming year, a year hence: faciendum est ad annum,: quem ad annum tribunum plebis videbam fore,.—
In annum.
For a year: prorogatum in annum im

perium est, : si quid Est (gnaws) animum, differs curandi tempus in annum? : provisae frugis in annum Copia,.—

In the next year, the next year: quod stercoratione faciunt in annum segetes meliores,.—
Per annos, year by year, yearly: arva per annos mutant, et superest ager,; so, per omnes annos,; .—
Omnibus annis, all the years, always, .—
Transf.
Poet., a part of a year, a season of the year: nunc frondent silvae, nunc formosissimus an-nus,now the forest is clothed with verdure, now the year is most beautiful,; so, pomifer annus,: hibernus annus,: Pisaeumque domus non aestuat annum, i. e. the summer (in which season of the year the Olympic games were celebrated at Pisa), .—
The produce of the year (poet. or in post-Aug. prose; cf. annona, I.),: agricolae annum flevere,; ; ; : nec arare terram aut exspectare annum,, ubi v. Rup.; cf. Schwarz ad .—
Time of life (poet.): Dum vernat sanguis, dum rugis integer annus,while your years are free from wrinkles,: vitae longus et annus erit,the years of life,.—
In polit. life, the age to which one must attain in order to be appointed to an office (cf. annalis, II.): quod hoc honore me adfecistis primā petitione, quod anno meo,: subito reliquit annum suum seseque in annum proximum transtulit,: qui anno suo petierint,; ; .—
In astronomy: annus magnus or mundanus, the period of time in which the constellations return to the same place; acc. to years; v. ; ; and Madv. ad .

la:adj:annuus.html:
annŭus, a, um, adj.
annus
.
That lasts a year or continues through a year, of a year's duration: penus,: tempus,: provincia,: magistratus,: reges,: imperium,: spatium,: cultura,: annui victus, et saep.—
That returns, recurs, or happens every year, yearly, annual.
Adj.: annuo in cursu, Att. ap. : tempora,: commutationes,changes of the seasons,: labor (agricolarum),: plenitudo annuae messis,: deponit flavas annua terra comas,: annua magnae Sacra refer Cereri,: annuos reditus non dabunt, Esdr. 4, 13: annuā vice,annually,: annuis vicibus,—Hence,
Subst.: annŭum, i, and more freq. in the plur.: annŭa, ōrum, n., an annuity, annual stipend, pension: publici servi annua accipiunt,; ; ; : si cui annuum relictum fuerit,; .

la:adj:annalis.html:
annālis, e, adj.
annus
.
Continuing a year, annual: tempus, cursus,; so ; .—
Relating to the year or the age: Lex Villia Annalis, the law passed B. C. 180 by L. Villius, which determined the age necessary for election to an office of state (for the quæstorship, 31; for the office of Ædile, 37; for the praetorship, 40; and for the consulship, 43 years): legibus annalibus grandiorem aetatem ad consulatum constituebant,; cf.: eo anno (573 A. U. C.) rogatio primum lata est ab L. Villio tribuno plebis, quot annos nati quemque magistratum peterent caperentque. Inde cognomen familiae inditum, ut annales appellarentur,; cf. also .—
annālis, is (abl. reg. annali, ; ; but annalei, Varr. ap. : annale,; v. Neue, Formenl. I. p. 224), subst. m. (sc. liber), most freq. in plur.: an-nāles, ium (sc. libri), an historical work, in which the occurrences of the year are chronologically recorded, chronicles, annals (diff. from historia, a philosophical narration. following the internal relation of events, Ver. Fl. ap. ; cf. ).
Spec., from the most ancient per. down to the time of the Gracchi, when a literature had been formed, each pontifex maximus wrote down the occurrences of his year on tablets, which were hung up in his dwelling for the information of the public. Such tablets, accordingly, received the name of Annales Maximi (not to be confounded with the Libri Pontificales sive Pontificii, which contained instructions and liturgies for the holy rites). See the class. passages, ; ; Fest. s. v. maximi, and cf. Creuz. ad ; ; Niebuhr, Rom. Hist. 1, 277 sq. From these sources the Rom. histt. drew, and hence called their works, in gen., Annales. The most renowned among the annalists of the ancient period are Q. Fabius Pictor, M. Porcius Cato, and L. Calpurnius Piso (cf. ); in the time of the emperors, Tacitus named one of his hist. works Annales, since in it the history of Rome, from the death of Aug. until the time of Nero, was given acc. to the annual succession of events; cf. Bähr, Lit. Gesch. p. 255 sq.; 301 sq.; 313 sq.; Teuffel, Rom. Lit. § 333, 1.—Annalis in sing., ; ; ; .—Adj., with liber, Ver. Fl. in the above-cited passage, and .—
In gen., records, archives, history: carminibus antiquis, quod unum apud illos memoriae et annalium genus est,: annalibus traditum (est) coram rege,: annales priorum temporum,.—
annālia, ium, n., a festival observed at the beginning of the year, .

an-no (better adn-), āre, v. n.
To swim to, toward, or along; constr. with the dat., ad, or acc.
With dat.: terrae,: ei insulae crocodili non adnant, Jan.—
With ad: ad litus,.—
With acc.: pauci milites, qui naves adnare possent,.—Absol.: plures adnabunt thynni, * .—
Trop.: quod ubique gentium est, ad eam urbem posset adnare,come to, approach,.—
To swim with or along with: pedites adnantes equis,.

la:adj:annosus.html:
annōsus, a, um, adj.
annus
,
of many years, aged, old (a favorite word of the Aug. poets and post-Aug. prose writers): anus,: vetustas,: merum,: bracchia,: robur,: ornus, al.: cornix,: palatum,: volumina vatum, (not elsewhere): gens, quos Hyperboreos appellavere, annoso degit aevo,; .—Comp., .—Sup., al.

la:verb:annoto.gloss: to put a note to, write down, note down; remark, comment on, state; annotate
la:verb:annoto.html:
an-nŏto (better adn-), āvi, ātum, 1, v. a.,
to put a note to something, to write down something, to note down, remark, comment on (only in post-Aug. prose, like its derivatives annotatio, annotator, annotamentum, etc.).
In gen.: ut meminisset atque adnotaret, quid et quando et cui dedisset,: in scriptis adnotare quaedam ut tumida,: liber legebatur, adnotabatur,; so : quā in re et aliud adnotare succurrit,: quod annales adnotavere,: de quibus in orthographiā pauca adnotabo,—Hence,
= animadvertere, to observe, perceive: cum adnotāsset insculptum monumento militem Gallum, etc.,.—
Adnotare librum, to give a book some title, to entitle, denominate: ausus est libros suos φιλαληθεῖς adnotare, —
Annotari, to be distinguished, noted for something: haec litora pisce nobili adnotantur,.—
Judic. t. t.
To enter or register an absent person among the accused: absens requirendus, adnotandus est, ut copiam sui praestet,.—
To note or designate one, already condemned, for punishment: quos, quia cives Romani erant, adnotavi in urbem remittendos,; so ; 7, 20; Schwarz; .

la:adj:anniversarius.html:
annĭversārĭus, a, um, adj.
annusverto
,
that returns, happens, is used, etc., every year, returning or renewed annually, annual, yearly: sacra,: Ecce solemnitas Domini est in Silo anniversaria,: festi dies,: (caeli) vicissitudines,the changes of the seasons of the year,; : arma,; so, hostes,: valetudines,: pervigilium,—Adv.: annĭversārĭē, annually,

la:verb:annuntio.gloss: to announce, make known, report, proclaim, relate
la:verb:annuntio.html:
an-nuntĭo (better adn-), not an-nuncĭo (adn-), āre, v. a.,
to announce, make known, relate, proclaim (post-Aug. and mostly eccl.; very freq. in Vulg.).
With acc. and inf.: adnuntiavere exanimatum illum,.—
With quod: adnuntiavit ei, quod occidisset Saül sacerdotes,.—
With ut and subj.: gentibus adnuntiabam, ut paenitentiam agerent,; .—
With acc.: adnuntiabo veritatem tuam,I will declare,: adnuntia regnum Dei,preach,: qui Evangelium adnuntiant,: adnuntiantes Dominum Jesum,; so, sic adnuntiabat,—
With acc. and dat.: bona regi adnuntiant,; ; .—
With de: adnuntiantes ei de puteo,; ib. Job, 36, 33; ; .

la:verb:annumero.gloss: to count to or out to, reckon, put into a person's account
la:verb:annumero.html:
an-nŭmĕro (better adn-), āvi, ātum, 1,
v. a.
Lit., to count to, to count out to, to put to a person's account: mihi talentum argenti adnumerat,: argentum, * : et reddere pecuniam mulieri,: senatus singulos denarios alicui,: non adnumerare verba sed appendere,: cuique sua,.—
To add to, to include with, reckon with.
With dat.: his libris adnumerandi sunt sex de re publicā,: his duobus adnumerabatur nemo tertius,; so ; ; .—
With in: in grege adnumeror,I am counted with, numbered with, the multitude,; ; .—Also
With inter: servos inter urbanos,.—
With cum (eccl. Lat.): adnumeratus est cum undecim apostolis,. —In Plin. also, to give the number of something: Mandorum nomen iis dedit trecentosque eorum vicos adnumerat,.—
Trop.
To attribute, impute to (only post-class.): imperitia culpae est adnumeranda,.—*
To reckon for, consider equal to: agni chordi duo pro uno ove adnumerantur,.

la:verb:annecto.gloss: to bind or tie to, connect, annex
la:verb:annecto.html:
an-necto (better adn-), nexui, nexum, 3, v. a.,
to tie or bind to, to connect, annex.
Lit.: (animum) corporibus nostris, * : funiculus scapham adnexam trahebat,: ad linguam stomachus adnectitur,; ap. : adnexa (ratis) erat vinculis,: continenti adnexuit,, where Jan reads adjecit: epistulae adnexae pedibus columbarum,; : remedia corporibus aegrorum,to apply,—
Trop.: rebus praesentibus adnectit futuras,: aliquod membrum adnexum orationi,; cf. .

la:noun:annona.gloss: yearly produce, yearly income, annual output
senses: yearly produce, yearly income, annual output
price of grain, or of some other food
la:noun:annona.html:
annōna, ae, f.
from annus, as pomona from pomum
.
In gen., the yearly produce, the annual income of natural products, in the widest sense (cf.: cibaria annua,): vectigal novum ex salariā annonā,: lactis,: musti,; .—
Esp.
Means of subsistence, and, for the most part, corn or grain: annona nisi in calamitate pretium non habet,: vilitas annonae ex summā inopiā et caritate rei frumentariae consecuta est,: uberrimus ager ad varietates annonae horreum populi Romani fore videbatur,: clausis annonae subsidiis,: provincia annonae fecunda,; cf. : annonae curam agere,; cf. : praebebant annonam regi,; ; —Sometimes contrasted with frumentum, as provisions in gen.: copia frumenti et annona tolerabilis rerum aliarum, a supply, Liv 35, 44.—
Meton., the price of grain or other food: quom cara annona sit,; ; ; : annona est gravis,; so : incendere annonam,: jam ad denarios quinquaginta in singulos modios annona pervenerat,: nihil mutavit annona, (cf. : annona vetus): annona acris,: gravitas annonae,: in annonae difficultatibus,: annona macelli,.—
Trop., the prices, the market: Qui homines probi essent, esset īs annona vilior,: Vilis amicorum est annona, bonis ubi quid deest,cheap indeed is the market of friendship,: his opibus numquam cara est annona veneni,.—Hence sometimes,
Dearness: cena hac annonā est sine sacris hereditas, at the present (i. e. high) market-price, at the present dear rate, : ob annonae causam,.—
In milit. lang., provisions, supplies: necessitas annonam pariter et arma portandi,: annona decem et septem dierum,.—Hence, meton., the loaves of bread them selves, rations (in this sense only in the plur.): ceteri annonas binas aut ternas accipiebant,

; cf. Cod. Th. 7,5.—

Personified, the goddess of the yearly produce: ANNONAE SANCTAE AELIVS VITALIO, etc.,.

annĭcŭlus, a, um, adj.
annus
,

la:verb:annuo.gloss: to favour or designate with a nod, to nod assent, approval, or consent; especially, as a sign of divine approval or favor
la:verb:annuo.html:
an-nŭo (better adn-), ŭi (ūvi, Enn. ap. P.), ūtum, 3, v. n.
-nuo, whence nutum; Gr. νεύω; cf. abnuo
,
to nod to, to nod.
In gen.: ne illa ulli homini nutet, nictet, adnuat,: adnuerunt sociis,: simul ac adnuisset,at the first nod,: adnuentibus ac vocantibus suis evadit,: adnuit, et totum nutu tremefecit Olympum,; to ask by a wink or nod (opp. renuo), .—
Esp.
To give assent or approval by nodding, to nod assent to, to approve, favor, allow, grant. promise to do (constr. with dat. of person, or with acc. of thing and dat. of person; opp. abnuo, to dissent, refuse): daturine estis an non? adnuunt,: adnuo Terram intuens modeste, * : id quoque toto capite adnuit,; : non adversata petenti Adnuit,: audacibus adnue coeptis,be favorable to, smile on our undertakings,; ; : amicitiis adnuere,: Adnuit precibus Lysiae,: Omnia omnibus adnuit,.—With acc. of thing: quod cum rex adnuisset, 4, 10.—With acc. and inf.: adnuvit sese mecum decernere ferro, Enn. ap. P.: ego autem venturum adnuo,; ; .—
Adnuere alicui aliquid; poet., to promise or grant something to one: caeli quibus adnuis arcem,: sin nostrum adnuerit nobis Victoria Martem,shall grant us a successful engagement,: ni divūm pater adnuisset rebus Aeneae potiore ductos alite muros,: adnuite nutum numenque vestrum invictum Campanis, give your assent, etc., .—
To designate a person or thing,
By a nod: quos iste adnuerat,.—
By a wink: quae adnuit oculo,; so absol.: adnuunt oculis,they make signs with their eyes,; ; .—
By the hand: adnuens eis manu, ut tacerent,: adnuit manu ad plebem,. —Hence, in gen., to indicate, declare: falsa adnuere,.

In gen., the yearly produce, the annual income of natural products, in the widest sense (cf.: cibaria annua,): vectigal novum ex salariā annonā,: lactis,: musti,; .—
Esp.
Means of subsistence, and, for the most part, corn or grain: annona nisi in calamitate pretium non habet,: vilitas annonae ex summā inopiā et caritate rei frumentariae consecuta est,: uberrimus ager ad varietates annonae horreum populi Romani fore videbatur,: clausis annonae subsidiis,: provincia annonae fecunda,; cf. : annonae curam agere,; cf. : praebebant annonam regi,; ; —Sometimes contrasted with frumentum, as provisions in gen.: copia frumenti et annona tolerabilis rerum aliarum, a supply, Liv 35, 44.—
Meton., the price of grain or other food: quom cara annona sit,; ; ; : annona est gravis,; so : incendere annonam,: jam ad denarios quinquaginta in singulos modios annona pervenerat,: nihil mutavit annona, (cf. : annona vetus): annona acris,: gravitas annonae,: in annonae difficultatibus,: annona macelli,.—
Trop., the prices, the market: Qui homines probi essent, esset īs annona vilior,: Vilis amicorum est annona, bonis ubi quid deest,cheap indeed is the market of friendship,: his opibus numquam cara est annona veneni,.—Hence sometimes,
Dearness: cena hac annonā est sine sacris hereditas, at the present (i. e. high) market-price, at the present dear rate, : ob annonae causam,.—
In milit. lang., provisions, supplies: necessitas annonam pariter et arma portandi,: annona decem et septem dierum,.—Hence, meton., the loaves of bread them selves, rations (in this sense only in the plur.): ceteri annonas binas aut ternas accipiebant,

; cf. Cod. Th. 7,5.—

Personified, the goddess of the yearly produce: ANNONAE SANCTAE AELIVS VITALIO, etc.,.
